demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette: John had always taken pride in his work as a bank teller. He was meticulous and careful, never wanting to make mistakes that could affect others. But one day, in a moment of distraction, he accidentally triggered the security system, causing a severe injury to a colleague who was caught off guard. The incident left John shaken, and over time, it began to unravel his sense of self. As he navigated his daily routine, John found himself on high alert, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. He had difficulty falling asleep at night, lying awake as his mind replayed the incident, rehashing what he could have done differently. Even in safe spaces, like his own home, John felt a persistent sense of unease, unable to shake the feeling that something was off. These feelings of hypervigilance and sleep vigilance made him feel like he was walking on eggshells, never knowing when the next trigger would set him off. When someone touched him unexpectedly, even his wife, John's nerves would fray. He couldn't explain why it affected him so deeply, but being caught off guard brought back the same terror he felt in those chaotic moments after the incident. His reactions since then only served to reinforce his growing sense of inadequacy – he was no longer the reliable, competent person he once thought himself to be. As John's self-doubt grew, memories of that fateful day began to surface more frequently, accompanied by crushing guilt and a deep-seated fear that he had permanently changed for the worse. These memories would often return unbidden, sudden pieces of the incident flashing before his eyes like snapshots. When they did, John felt himself transported back to the scene, reliving the horror and panic. His mind told him he was in danger, that something terrible was about to happen again, and this conviction only intensified his hypervigilance. As these fragments resurfaced, John's perception of himself as a "lousy coper" solidified – why else would these memories still have such power over him? This self-perception, in turn, heightened his sensitivity to triggers: related people, stress, and unexpected touch all took on a menacing quality. At work, John found it increasingly difficult to interact with customers or even his own family. His wife noticed the change in him, but he couldn't explain why he was so distant, so preoccupied. Even simple tasks like counting money or answering questions made him anxious, as if he were waiting for the other shoe to drop. As these difficulties accumulated, John began to see himself as irreparably damaged – a permanent victim of his own carelessness. This sense of hopelessness finally brought him to seek help, though what frightened him most was that therapy would reveal even more evidence of his inadequacy. John's greatest fear now is that he will never be able to shake the memories of that incident or quiet the voice that tells him he's a failure. He hopes that with therapy, he can learn to calm the hypervigilance and rebuild some semblance of control over his life – but for now, those goals feel as elusive as ever.
